repos.title: TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate
repos.paper_summary:
TurboQuant is an online vector quantization method that achieves near-optimal distortion rates for both mean-squared error (MSE) and inner product estimation. The algorithm first applies a random rotation to input vectors, inducing a Beta distribution on coordinates. It then uses precomputed optimal scalar quantizers derived from a continuous k-means problem to encode each coordinate independently. For unbiased inner product estimation, the method combines an MSE-optimized quantizer with a 1-bit Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform applied to the residual vector.

The paper proves that for any bit-width $b$, TurboQuant’s MSE distortion is bounded by $\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{4^b}$, which is within a factor of approximately 2.7 of the information-theoretic lower bound. The inner product distortion is bounded by $\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi^2 \|y\|_2^2}{d} \cdot \frac{1}{4^b}$. Experiments on KV cache quantization show quality neutrality at 3.5 bits per channel and marginal degradation at 2.5 bits. In nearest neighbor search, TurboQuant outperforms existing product quantization techniques in recall while reducing indexing time to zero. Limitations include the requirement for unit-norm inputs, though non-unit norms can be handled by storing separate scaling factors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: TurboQuant combines an MSE-optimal rotation-based quantizer with a 1-bit QJL residual stage to get unbiased, near-optimal inner product quantization.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Coordinates of a uniform hypersphere point follow a Beta law that tends to a normal law, and QJL gives an unbiased single-bit estimator.

digest_headlines.heading: TurboQuant: High Performance Quantization
digest_headlines.headline: MSE distortion is bounded by a constant times 1/4^b, reaching 0.36 at 1 bit and 0.009 at 4 bits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: TurboQuant matches full-precision performance on needle-in-a-haystack, and outperforms product quantization in recall while reducing indexing time to essentially zero.

repos.title: Constraint Breeds Generalization: Temporal Dynamics as an Inductive Bias
repos.paper_summary: This paper argues that dissipative temporal dynamics, meaning phase-space contraction, act as an inductive bias that improves generalization in spiking neural networks (SNNs). Static features are converted into time series by a Duffing oscillator whose parameter δ sets the dynamics as expansive (δ<0), transition (δ≈0 to 2), or dissipative. Leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with leak β provide an architecture-level variant. On handwritten digits (64 features, 10 classes), SNNs trained in the transition regime generalize across a 12×12 matrix of encodings, while expansive-trained networks fail outside their training encoding. On CIFAR-10 patches, the transition regime yields localized, oriented receptive fields (structure score 0.206, versus 0.0541 for the best alternative in Table 1). Experiment 3 reports zero-shot transfer to unseen physical environments in reinforcement learning that beats baseline architectures. Limitations include fixed oscillator and fixed β parameters, and generality is checked only on a few alternative dynamical systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hypothesizes that dissipative temporal dynamics act as an inductive bias for generalization, tested at representational, structural, and behavioral levels.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Controls phase-space contraction through a single oscillator parameter δ for static inputs and neuron leak β for temporal inputs.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Argues the transition regime trades fit for stability; the authors flag fixed parameters and untested regime generality as limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Concludes that dissipative dynamics are an inductive bias, so generalization may depend on dynamical regime as much as on scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists oscillator equations and parameters, a dynamical indicator table, experiment details, Bayesian bound and gradient analyses, and extra figures.

repos.title: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives
repos.paper_summary:
GroundingPI is a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that outputs points and boxes as quantized coordinate tokens in a shared vocabulary. It is trained with multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO reinforcement learning. On 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, it averages 73.68% against 44 baselines, above GPT-6 Astra at 71.54%. Metrics are F1 with mIoU for boxes and OCR, F1 at point for pointing, and task accuracy otherwise. As a visual backbone in a shared flow-matching action head, it outperforms every evaluated mainstream backbone in four out-of-distribution RoboTwin 2.0 settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest. On RoboCasa-GR1 it reaches baseline-level results with 50% of demonstrations versus 75% for the baselines. On nuScenes trajectory prediction it reaches an open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. Driving uses a language-token trajectory interface with cross-entropy training.

The paper reports gaps on tiny-box localization, high-IoU boundaries, TotalText OCR, FSC147 visual prompting, and GUI grounding. Baseline prompt and parser incompatibilities limit several comparisons, and the manipulation pretrained backbones differ in scale and supervision. Driving is evaluated open loop only.

repos.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
repos.paper_summary:
DSPy is a programming model that compiles declarative language model pipelines into self-improving systems by automatically optimizing prompts and demonstrations. It replaces hard-coded prompt strings with parameterized modules, such as `ChainOfThought` or `ReAct`, which are optimized by "teleprompters." These optimizers bootstrap few-shot examples or finetune smaller models to maximize a user-defined metric.

On the GSM8K math word problem dataset, compiled DSPy programs using GPT-3.5 achieved 81.6% test accuracy, outperforming standard few-shot prompting (72.4%) and expert-created demonstrations (72.4%). For llama2-13b-chat, the best configuration reached 46.9% test accuracy, surpassing the zero-shot baseline of 9.4%. On HotPotQA multi-hop question answering, a compiled multi-hop program with GPT-3.5 achieved 45.6% answer exact match, while a finetuned T5-Large model reached 39.3% on the development set. The paper notes that compiling typically takes minutes to tens of minutes. Limitations include reliance on specific metrics for optimization and the fact that results are reported on only two case studies.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hand-written prompt templates for LM pipelines are brittle, and the paper proposes DSPy to replace them with optimizable modules.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing toolkits rely on hand-written prompt templates, while DSPy aims to optimize arbitrary multi-stage LM pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Programming Model
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy programs combine typed signatures, parameterized modules, and teleprompters that optimize all modules against a metric.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Compiler
digest_headlines.headline: The compiler runs three stages: bootstrapping candidate demonstrations, selecting among them, and optimizing control flow.

digest_headlines.heading: Goals of Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation hypothesizes that DSPy can replace hand-written prompts without losing quality, adapt across LMs, and enable richer pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy supports rapid development of effective systems with small LMs, and wider task reporting is deferred to future work.

digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers advanced signatures, a comparison with LangChain and LlamaIndex, and long prompts from existing libraries and DSPy.

repos.title: Reactive Optimizers
repos.paper_summary: Reactive Optimizers presents OPAL, a method in which a pretrained language-model agent watches one training run and rewrites executable optimizer code (`updater.py`) and its own diagnostic program (`analysis.py`) during training, with no meta-training or cross-run memory. Across language modeling and image generation settings where no recipe was tuned, OPAL matches or beats the selected fixed recipes. On Goldfish Amharic, bits per sentence on FLORES-200 fall from 83.48 for the official recipe to 81.11 for OPAL. On LightningDiT-XL/1, FID-50K with guidance drops from 2.18 to 1.83. In a CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 run with 10% wrong labels, OPAL reaches test loss 0.685 against 2.493 for final AdamW weights. Changes include mid-run learning-rate increases, switching some matrices to Muon, and keeping one embedding matrix in float32. Wall-clock overhead is 1.01× to 1.14× when training does not wait for the agent. Limitations stated by the authors: gains are smaller on the heavily tuned modded-nanogpt task, and reactive edits may reduce reproducibility. Most runs were done once or three times.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed optimizer recipes cannot respond to training incidents, so the paper proposes an optimizer that rewrites itself during one run.

digest_headlines.heading: Training without a recipe
digest_headlines.headline: Without tuned recipes, OPAL matches or beats the best baseline in every new setting tested, including Amharic at 81.11 against 83.48.

digest_headlines.heading: Updating with spontaneous analysis
digest_headlines.headline: OPAL writes two programs: one rewrites the update code, and one chooses which training statistics to observe during the run.

digest_headlines.heading: What is dynamically changing during optimization?
digest_headlines.headline: Logged decisions show OPAL changing learning-rate schedules, optimizer assignments, precision, momentum, clipping, and data gating during training.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-world applicability
digest_headlines.headline: Letting training continue while the agent reasons adds 1.01× to 1.14× wall-clock time, and gains shrink on short, tuned runs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Most runs ended ahead of their starting recipes, and the authors argue reactive optimizers suit settings where no recipe exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists related work on learned and adaptive optimizers, the overfitting setup, and decision records for the runs.

repos.title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
repos.paper_summary:
LoongSage is an agent-native reinforcement learning framework for LLM post-training, built on Megatron for training and SGLang for inference, with about 14K lines of core code. Its AgentFlow layer serves agents through a Chat Completions interface and stores trajectories at the token level (Token-In, Token-Out), so sampled and trained sequences match. Black-box agents with context compaction or subagents are stored as a segment tree, and only mainline segments are trained. Three sliding-window policies bound staleness in fully asynchronous mode: no-window, window-gated (staleness at most S steps), and windowed-fifo (collection limited to one batch). TransferMesh selects a weight-transfer transport per receiver topology, such as CUDA IPC for colocated GPUs or NCCL for distributed nodes. A Teacher Manager supports multi-teacher on-policy distillation with sampled-token, top-K, full-vocabulary, and JSD estimators.

The evidence is four complete training runs, reported as steady task-reward improvement, a controlled train–inference gap, and reduced idle time. The paper does not provide a theorem. Its limitations include multi-agent credit assignment, which is left as non-trainable placeholders, and support for proprietary agent APIs, which is still under development.

digest_headlines.headline: Existing RL frameworks add overhead for agentic training, so the paper proposes LoongSage, built on Megatron and SGLang.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work

digest_headlines.heading: The LoongSage Framework
digest_headlines.headline: The architecture uses one controller over Ray actors, token-level internal interfaces, and seven planes, with three of four placement combinations supported.

digest_headlines.heading: Key Features
digest_headlines.headline: AgentFlow stores white-box and black-box agent trajectories as token arrays and segment trees, and three sliding-window policies bound asynchronous staleness.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Four training runs show rising rewards with bounded train–inference gaps, and asynchronous execution gives a 1.35× speedup.

digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion lists six contributions and plans to add Proximal Policy Optimization, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Low-Rank Adaptation.

repos.title: PhysAg3D: Bridging 3D Generative and Agentic Models for High-Fidelity and Physically-Interactive Assets
repos.paper_summary: PhysAg3D generates interactive 3D assets from a single image by coupling a pretrained 3D generator with a vision-language agent that builds executable physical models. The agent infers semantic and physical priors from the image, while TRELLIS.2 produces a textured whole-object mesh. A hierarchical representation links requirements, physical mechanisms (rigid joints or compliant domains), and the visible surfaces that implement them. The agent constructs parts, joints, and surface bindings, then revises them using rendered views and MuJoCo execution checks, with at most two builder repairs. On 50 in-the-wild objects with 110 actions, PhysAg3D reaches 91.3% Action Completion Rate and 88.0% Function-and-Visible-Stability Pass, versus 66.8% and 42.0% for the strongest baseline, aDSL. On PhysXVerse and PhysX-Mobility it improves PSNR over the strongest baseline by 2.74 and 2.76 dB. The paper states that recovering hidden structure and material properties remains a limitation. Stability is judged from rendered video, not simulator logs, and ear-pad compliance uses an approximate model.

repos.title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation
repos.paper_summary: Hy-Nomas is an 8B-parameter video world model that generates interactive video from free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple turns. It is built on HunyuanVideo 1.5 and generates variable-length segments conditioned on the current input and cached history. Its main design choice is action-aware causal attention: structured captions describe persistent scene and subject context that stays visible to later segments, while timestamped action instructions are limited to their own time window. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and interaction history into structured conditions for each next segment. Training follows a multi-stage curriculum (causal generation, text interaction, camera control, training on model-generated histories), then diffusion distillation. Human evaluation is reported as favoring Hy-Nomas over existing world models, but the text provided does not include the scores. The paper notes that temporal causality does not establish physical causality, that robotics adaptation is shown only as an initial LoRA demonstration, and that retrieving past views does not update off-screen state, such as a clock that should keep running. Weights, code, and benchmarks are released.

repos.title: FinRL: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Library for Automated Stock Trading in Quantitative Finance
repos.paper_summary:
FinRL is an open-source Python library for automated stock trading using deep reinforcement learning. It structures the workflow into three layers: a market environment simulator, a set of pre-configured DRL agents, and application modules for single-stock, multi-stock, and portfolio allocation tasks. The environment layer models trading as a Markov Decision Process using historical data from six indices (NASDAQ-100, DJIA, S&P 500, HSI, SSE 50, CSI 300) at daily, hourly, or minute granularity. Agents include DQN, DDPG, PPO, SAC, A2C, and TD3, built on OpenAI Baselines and Stable Baselines.

The library incorporates market frictions such as transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, and a turbulence index to control risk during extreme volatility. Backtesting uses the `pyfolio` package. In demonstrations over 2019–2020 data, PPO-based single-stock strategies achieved Sharpe ratios between 1.10 and 1.49, outperforming the S&P 500 baseline of 0.74. For DJIA constituents, TD3 and DDPG strategies yielded Sharpe ratios of 1.38 and 1.28, respectively, exceeding the min-variance baseline of 0.44. Limitations include reliance on historical data that may not reflect future market regimes and the computational cost of training multiple agent configurations.
